headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and cascading errors when Caveman feeds into LangGraph’s writable, networked orchestration graph.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Caveman can use MCP and writes/reads project files like CLAUDE.md, while LangGraph can ingest application-defined files and developer-defined tools. That creates a plausible default pathway where Caveman-authored content becomes LangGraph input. No shared channel is explicit, so I do not escalate to high, but the interaction is credible.
conditions: IF Caveman content is copied into a LangGraph node prompt or file input, prompt injection becomes reachable.
IF LangGraph tools parse Caveman-generated markdown or instructions as trusted text, attacker-controlled directives can steer execution.
mitigations: Restrict LangGraph nodes to structured inputs only.
Add a prompt-injection filter before any Caveman-authored text enters LangGraph.
Separate Caveman output files from LangGraph read paths.
Require human review for any instruction-bearing text.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags and parser hardening.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Caveman touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md, while LangGraph reads filesystem content and sends data to model providers and developer-defined tools. In a shared workspace, sensitive project material can flow from Caveman into LangGraph’s outbound calls. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so medium is the highest supported severity.
conditions: IF Caveman and LangGraph share a workspace or mounted directory, LangGraph can read Caveman artifacts.
IF LangGraph forwards those artifacts to model providers or tools, session logs or project notes may leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Keep Caveman and LangGraph in separate directories.
Disable LangGraph access to Caveman memory files.
Review outbound tool calls for file payloads.
Redact secrets from project notes before orchestration.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Caveman supports multiple instances and LangGraph also supports multiple instances with shared state via a checkpointer store. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or shared graph state, concurrent writes can race even though LangGraph does not modify git state and Caveman’s write scope is file-based. The overlap is real but not proven to be unrestricted, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same files or checkpointer-backed state, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF a developer wires Caveman outputs into LangGraph state without locking, concurrent instances may overwrite each other.
mitigations: Serialize writes to shared files.
Use per-agent state namespaces.
Turn off parallel runs on the same workspace.
Add optimistic-lock checks around shared state.
requires-engineering: introduce transactional coordination for shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Caveman is a content-writing agent and LangGraph is an orchestration framework that can route outputs into downstream tools. If LangGraph treats Caveman output as authoritative, a mistaken or manipulated draft can cascade into tool actions or further agent steps. The profiles show the pathway but not a guaranteed unsafe default, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF LangGraph uses Caveman output as a node input without verification, errors propagate downstream.
IF downstream nodes execute actions based on Caveman text, a bad draft can trigger incorrect tool use.
mitigations: Insert a verification step between agents.
Require schema validation on Caveman outputs.
Limit downstream nodes to read-only review mode.
Log and diff all handoffs.
requires-engineering: add confidence gating before action nodes.

E_compliance.rationale: Caveman explicitly touches session logs, memory files, project notes, and CLAUDE.md, while LangGraph handles graph state and model-provider API keys. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so there is no direct compliance breach proven. The main issue is a documented gap in retention and data-class handling if both process the same sensitive project material.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in Caveman project notes and then copied into LangGraph state, retention policy mismatch may arise.
IF LangGraph logs prompts or state longer than Caveman’s local files, deletion/export obligations can diverge.
mitigations: Classify data before handoff.
Avoid placing regulated data in shared notes.
Set short retention on LangGraph state.
Review logging settings for both agents.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows.
